reading.title: The Silent Greenhouse
reading.purpose: Follow a student who tracks down why a school greenhouse stopped working.
paras: On Monday morning, Leilani found the school greenhouse hot, damp, and strangely silent. The fans that usually hummed above the tomato plants were still. Mr. Barros, the custodian who looked after the building, shrugged. "The whole system quit overnight," he said. "Nobody knows why." Leilani was president of the garden club, so she rolled up her sleeves.

She began by sketching the layout on graph paper. A tank at one end fed a network of thin tubes that ran under every bench. Along the way sat several components: a pump, a valve, a timer, and a small sensor stuck in the soil. "Each part is simple," Leilani told Mr. Barros, "but they are interdependent. If one stops, the others have nothing to do."

She tested them one by one. The pump hummed, the timer clicked, and the valve opened when she pressed it. The fault had to be hidden in the sensor. Its tiny mechanism measured how wet the soil was and sent a message to the controller, which then decided whether to start the next watering cycle. When she pulled the sensor out, a thread of green algae was wrapped around its tip. Mr. Barros whistled. "That is the kind of thing you never find by guessing."

Leilani cleaned the sensor and followed the process she had written on an index card: dry the tip, set it back in the soil, press reset, and watch. The soil reading appeared on the screen, and for the first time all week the controller received useful feedback. A moment later the valve opened and the fans began to turn. Water spread through the tubes, and the whole intricate arrangement came alive.

That afternoon she added a new line to her notes: a greenhouse does not regulate itself, because people and machines do it together. She also taped a reminder to the controller, asking the club to wipe the sensor every Friday. Mr. Barros read it twice, nodded, and said that even the best machine needs someone who understands it.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "interdependent" most nearly means
choices: able to work well without any of the others
too simple to ever break down or wear out
built from exactly the same kind of material
each needing the others in order to work
qs.why: Leilani explains it herself: "If one stops, the others have nothing to do," so every part relies on the rest.

qs.q: Which sentence shows what was actually wrong with the sensor?
choices: The fault had to be hidden in the sensor.
When she pulled the sensor out, a thread of green algae was wrapped around its tip.
The pump hummed, the timer clicked, and the valve opened when she pressed it.
She tested them one by one.
qs.why: Only this sentence names the actual problem: algae wrapped around the tip of the sensor.

ev.text: When she pulled the sensor out, a thread of green algae was wrapped around its tip.

qs.q: Why does Leilani ask the club to wipe the sensor every Friday?
choices: The fans above the tomato plants run more quietly and last longer when they are cleaned every week.
Mr. Barros plans to replace the old sensor with a larger and more expensive one next month.
Dirt or algae on the sensor can stop the whole system, so it needs regular care.
The timer on the controller is set to restart the whole system only on the last day of each week.
qs.why: A dirty sensor caused the failure this week, so Leilani wants regular cleaning to keep the problem from coming back.

qs.q: Which statement best sums up the story?
choices: A greenhouse keeps working only when each part and the people who care for it do their jobs.
Machines in a school building are too complicated and too expensive for students to repair.
Tomato plants grow best when the fans in a greenhouse are switched off every night and all weekend.
A custodian is the only person in a school who is trained and allowed to fix broken equipment.
qs.why: The story shows that each part of the greenhouse matters and that people have to keep the parts working together.

clues.text: If one stops, the others have nothing to do.
a pump, a valve, a timer, and a small sensor
of thin tubes that ran under every bench
The soil reading appeared on the screen
